 singapore At least $1.3m lost to Simba staff impersonation scam in October, police warn
 At least 59 cases have been reported since the start of October, with scammers posing as Simba staff before transferring victims to accomplices impersonating police or MAS officers If you are told that you have purchased iPhones or subscribed to mobile plans or packages by person(s) claiming to be from telco Simba, do not continue the call. PHOTO: AsiaOne/Danial Zahrin PUBLISHED ON October 29, 2026 11:22 AM BY Sean Ler Members of the public should be wary of scams involving fraudsters posing as staff from telco Simba.
 In an advisory issued on Thursday (Oct 29) afternoon, police said there have been at least 59 cases reported in October, with losses amounting to at least $1.3 million.
 In these cases, victims received unsolicited calls from scammers claiming to be from Simba.
 The victims were told by the "employees" that they had purchased iPhones or subscribed to mobile plans or packages with the telco.
 Modus operandi: The same red flags
 When the victims denied making such purchases, the scammers would claim that the victims' personal details had been misused and that further investigations were required. 
 This modus operandi is similar to that of scams involving fraudsters impersonating Harvey Norman or M1 staff . 
 In all such cases, victims were then transferred to another scammer impersonating police or Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) officers, who would then instruct the victims to transfer money to bank accounts, or hand over cash and/or valuables to purported police or MAS officers for the purpose of "investigations".
 In some past cases, victims would be reassured that their money and valuables would be returned to them once these "investigations" were completed.
 Victims would only realise that they had been scammed after the scammers became uncontactable or when victims sought verification from the relevant government agencies.
 How to guard against these red flags
 While scammers are known to apply pressure tactics, those who receive such calls are advised to stay calm and spot these signs:
 Asking for cash, gold, luxury watches, or cryptocurrency to be transferred or handed over.
 Asking for banking login details.
 Asking to obtain loans from licensed moneylenders.
 Installing mobile apps from unverified app stores.
 Transferring calls to the police or other government officials.
 Those who find themselves in such situations should stop acceding to requests of scammers and seek advice from the authorities, family members or friends.
 If in doubt, members of the public can call the 24/7 ScamShield helpline at 1799 for assistance.
 Later this year, calls from the police will start with a common, easily recognisable prefix as part of efforts to counter such impersonation scams.
 The police will be the first government agency to pilot this initiative .
